## 1. Data and measurement

Sales, fitted values, residuals, innovations, and forecast errors all use estimated firearms per month unless otherwise specified as a scale of thousands or millions.

**Observational unit.** Each row is the background-check count for one area in one calendar month. For example, the Maryland row for January 2000 covers that state for the whole month. Each of the four areas has 192 consecutive months, so the data have **`r shape[1]` rows, `r shape[2]` original variables, and `r missing` missing values**. The date checks also confirm one row per area per month.

**Meaning of Totals.** The `Totals` row is the U.S. total for that month. It already includes Missouri, Maryland, New Jersey, and the rest of the country, so adding the three state rows would count those states twice. Questions 2–8 use the 192 national rows.

**Why $Y_t$ is an estimate.** The response is $Y_t=1.1(H_t+L_t)+2M_t^*$, where $H_t$ and $L_t$ count handgun and long-gun checks, and $M_t^*$ counts corrected multiple-firearm checks. Two things make it an estimate. First, the weights assume a number of firearms per check, and the data do not record how many firearms were actually bought. Second, some private sales never produce a check. The calculation also leaves out permit checks and the inconsistent California multiple-check data from the national multiple-firearm category (Aisch and Keller, 2016).

For January 2000, the national row gives $1.1(185{,}677+322{,}777)+2(7{,}826)=574{,}951.4$ estimated firearms. The decimal comes from the conversion weights. After sorting the national rows by date, we use January 2000–December 2014 for fitting and model selection (180 months) and January–December 2015 for forecast evaluation (12 months).

## 2. The national series

```{r national}
style()
plot(d$date, d$y/1e6, type="l", col=teal, lwd=1.4, xlab="Year",
     ylab="Sales (million firearms/month)",
     main="Estimated monthly U.S. firearm sales, 2000-2015")
abline(v=as.Date("2015-01-01"), lty=3, col=dark)
```

Mean monthly sales rose unevenly from `r fmt(mean(d$y[d$year==2000]))` in 2000 to `r fmt(mean(train$y[train$year==2014]))` in 2014. They were about 588,000 in 2003, peaked at 1.28 million in 2013, and then dipped slightly. Sales also jump late in the year, with spikes in December 2012 (2.39 million), January 2013 (1.90 million), and December 2015 (2.35 million). The dotted line marks the start of the 2015 holdout.

Because a stationary ARMA model requires a constant mean, constant variance, and lag-dependent autocovariances, it cannot be applied directly to this raw series. The overall level drifts upward through 2013 rather than reverting to a fixed mean, which would cause an ARMA forecast to pull unrealistically back toward the historical average. The series also displays strong calendar seasonality—peaking every December and dropping in the summer—creating annual correlations that a standard ARMA model isn't built to handle, alongside expanding variance where recent spikes dwarf earlier fluctuations. Fitting ARMA to the raw data would mostly capture this long-term trend and seasonal cycle rather than short-term dependence, so we estimate and remove the trend and month effects first (Question 4) before modeling the remaining residuals.

## 3. The annual sales pattern

Mean monthly estimated sales in **thousands of firearms per month**, January 2000–December 2014 (15 observations per month):

```{r monthly, results='asis'}
means <- tapply(train$y, train$month, mean)
tab <- as.data.frame(t(round(means/1000)))
names(tab) <- month.abb
tableout(tab)
```

```{r seasonal-spread, fig.height=2.4}
style()
boxplot(I(y/1e6) ~ month, data=train, names=month.abb,
        xlab="Calendar month", ylab="Sales (million firearms/month)",
        main="U.S. sales by calendar month, 2000-2014",
        col="#D8EBED", border=dark, outline=TRUE)
points(12, train$y[train$date==as.Date("2012-12-01")]/1e6,
       pch=1, cex=1.6, lwd=1.8, col=rust)
```

The bolded line in each box is the median of that month's 15 training observations, and the box spans the middle half of the values. The red ring marks December 2012. Comparing medians checks whether the seasonal gap persists when an extreme observation has little influence. The December median is `r fmt(median(train$y[train$month.num==12]))` firearms, compared to `r fmt(median(train$y[train$month.num==6]))` in June. These summaries mix early and late years, so we estimate the calendar effect while also accounting for the time trend in Question 4.

December had the highest average and was the annual maximum in `r sum(tapply(train$y,train$year,which.max)==12)` of 15 years. November was next, and June and July were nearly tied for lowest. A seasonal effect repeats at the same time every year, which is what we see here. December 2012 was `r fmt((d$y[d$date=="2012-12-01"]-means[12])/1e6,2)` million above the typical training December, so an unusual month can land on a seasonal peak. Without it, the other 14 training Decembers still averaged `r fmt(mean(train$y[train$month.num==12 & train$year!=2012]))` firearms per month. So both statements hold: December is usually high, and December 2012 was high even for a December. Means are above medians in most months because the spikes pull the means up. This is also why the boxplot shows high outliers.

## 4. Removing trend and seasonality

```{r decomposition, include=FALSE}
linear <- lm(y ~ t + month, data=train)
r <- as.numeric(resid(linear))
# Lecture 9 diagnostics on the chronological linear-model training residuals.
diagnose <- function(y) {
  n <- length(y)
  stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(y))
  pairs <- sum(vapply(2:n, function(i) sum(y[i] > y[seq_len(i-1)]), integer(1)))
  mu <- n*(n-1)/4
  sd.pairs <- sqrt(n*(n-1)*(2*n+5)/72)
  z.rank <- (pairs-mu)/sd.pairs
  rho <- as.numeric(acf(y, lag.max=24, plot=FALSE)$acf)[-1]
  lags <- c(1,12,24)
  z <- sqrt(n)*rho[lags]
  Q <- n*sum(rho^2)
  list(pairs=pairs, z.rank=z.rank, p.rank=2*pnorm(-abs(z.rank)),
       rho=rho[lags], z=z, p.lag=2*pnorm(-abs(z)),
       Q=Q, p.Q=pchisq(Q,df=24,lower.tail=FALSE))
}
checks <- lapply(list(Linear=r), diagnose)
```

On the 180 training months, the required least-squares model is
$$\widehat Y_t=461{,}145+3{,}668.15t+\widehat\gamma_{m(t)},\quad \widehat\gamma_{\rm Jan}=0,$$

where $t=1$ in January 2000. With the month effect held fixed, the fitted baseline grows by 3,668 estimated firearms per month, or about 44,018 per year. After controlling for time, December is +436,980 firearms above January. December is also 11 months after January in the same year, so the within-year gap is $436{,}980+11(3{,}668.15)\approx477{,}330$ estimated firearms.

```{r residual-comparison, fig.height=2.4}
style()
plot(train$date, r/1000, type="l", lwd=1.2, col=teal,
     main="U.S. sales residuals after linear trend and month adjustment",
     xlab="Calendar year", ylab="Residual (1,000 firearms/month)")
abline(h=0, col="gray55", lty=2)
```

A residual is observed sales minus the fitted value for that month. One isolated spike is acceptable. Several years of errors in the same direction mean the trend shape needs attention. The mean residual was positive in each of 2000–2002 and negative in every year from 2003 through 2011, so the constant slope leaves runs of overprediction and underprediction. The training root mean squared residual is `r fmt(sqrt(mean(r^2)))` estimated firearms per month. We carry these deviations into Questions 5–8.

Following Lecture 9 (Assessing the Residuals), we use three checks on the 180 training residuals at $\alpha=0.05$. The rank test looks for drift over time. The sample ACF tests look for correlation at specific lags. The Box–Pierce test looks for leftover correlation across many lags. The rank and ACF tests are two-sided because both positive and negative departures matter. Box–Pierce adds up squared correlations, so only a large positive value rejects.

**1. Remaining trend: rank test.** Under $H_0$, the residuals are iid from a continuous distribution, so a later residual is equally likely to be above or below an earlier one. The alternative is a systematic upward or downward tendency. In time order we count $\Pi=\sum_{i>j}I(r_i>r_j)$. With 16,110 pairs, the null mean is $\mu=n(n-1)/4=8{,}055$ and the null standard deviation is $s=\sqrt{n(n-1)(2n+5)/72}$. The residuals have no ties. The statistic is $Z=(\Pi-\mu)/s$, with approximate two-sided p-value $2\Phi(-|Z|)$.

```{r rank-results, results='asis'}
tableout(data.frame(Fit=names(checks), Pairs=sapply(checks, "[[", "pairs"),
  Z=fmt(sapply(checks,"[[","z.rank"),3),
  'Two-sided p'=fmt(sapply(checks,"[[","p.rank"),4),check.names=FALSE))
```

There are 7,336 increasing pairs, so $Z=-1.779$ and $p=0.0752$. We fail to reject $H_0$ at 0.05, so no statistically significant monotone trend is left. The count is a little below the expected 8,055, which means the linear trend and month effects removed most of the drift.

However, a borderline p-value alongside a curved residual pattern—positive from 2000–2002 and negative from 2003–2011—shows that slow curvature remains, as an initial drop followed by a rise cancels out in the rank test's pairwise counts. Although the residuals are stationary enough to move forward with ARMA modeling in Question 5, this leftover curvature inflates the lag-1 ACF (0.846) and slows its decay, forcing the ARMA component to absorb part of the trend. Furthermore, because ARMA forecasts revert to zero after a few months, longer-horizon predictions depend entirely on the linear baseline and inherit its bias—a limitation seen in Question 8 when the straight line overshoots early 2015.

**2. Remaining annual dependence: fixed-lag ACF tests.** We chose lags 12 and 24 because they compare the same calendar month one and two years apart. Lag 1 is a short-run comparison. For each lag $j$, $H_0:\rho(j)=0$ versus $H_1:\rho(j)\ne0$. The sample ACF $\hat\rho(j)$ is the lag-$j$ sample autocovariance divided by the lag-zero autocovariance. Under the lecture's iid finite-variance reference, $Z_j=\sqrt{180}\,\hat\rho(j)$ is approximately standard normal and $p_j=2\Phi(-|Z_j|)$. The matching pointwise 5% cutoff is $|\hat\rho(j)|>0.146$.

```{r lag-results, results='asis'}
lag.rows <- lapply(names(checks), function(name) {
  x <- checks[[name]]
  data.frame(Fit=name, Lag=c(1,12,24), ACF=fmt(x$rho,3), Z=fmt(x$z,3),
             p=formatC(x$p.lag,format="g",digits=3))
})
tableout(do.call(rbind,lag.rows))
```

**3. Remaining serial dependence: Box–Pierce test.** We use $h=24$ to cover two annual cycles and the months between. Under $H_0$, $\rho(1),\ldots,\rho(24)$ all equal zero. Under $H_1$, at least one does not. The lecture statistic is $Q=180\sum_{j=1}^{24}\hat\rho(j)^2$, and we use its approximate right-tail probability $P(\chi^2_{24}\ge Q)$. Question 7 tests the fitted ARMA innovations separately with Ljung–Box, which adjusts for the estimated coefficients.

```{r joint-results, results='asis'}
tableout(data.frame(Fit=names(checks), Q=fmt(sapply(checks,"[[","Q"),2),
                    df=24, p=formatC(sapply(checks,"[[","p.Q"),format="g",digits=3)))
```

The joint test strongly rejects independence at the 5% level ($Q=402.91$, 24 df), driven by a large positive lag-1 autocorrelation of 0.846. The month indicators force each calendar month's mean residual to zero, but observations a year apart still tend to miss their fitted values in the same direction, with significant lag-12 correlation being 0.288 ($p=0.000111$). By lag 24 it fades to 0.052 ($p=0.484$), so slow baseline shifts could explain part of the one-year correlation.

## 5. Stationarity and remaining correlation

A weakly stationary process has finite second moments, a constant mean, a covariance $\operatorname{Cov}(R_t,R_{t+h})=\gamma(h)$ depending only on lag $h$, and a constant variance $\gamma(0)$ (course notes, Chapters 1–2). The linear residual series in Question 4 varies around zero without the original upward drift. However, multi-year runs of errors with the same sign and larger late fluctuations raise slight doubts about a constant mean and variance, indicating that while a good portion of trend and seasonality has been eliminated reasonably well, it has not completed been removed. A correlation at lag 12 is compatible with weak stationarity if it recurs with the same strength over time.

```{r correlations, fig.height=2.4}
corplot <- function(x, partial=FALSE, title="", L=24) {
  values <- if (partial) as.numeric(pacf(x,lag.max=L,plot=FALSE)$acf) else
    as.numeric(acf(x,lag.max=L,plot=FALSE)$acf)[-1]
  plot(seq_len(L), values, type="h", lwd=1.7, col=teal, main=title, cex.main=.95,
       xlab="Lag (months)", ylab=if(partial) "Partial ACF (unitless)" else "ACF (unitless)",
       ylim=range(c(-.25,.25,values)), xaxs="i", xlim=c(0,L+1))
  abline(h=0,col=dark)
  abline(h=c(-1,1)*1.96/sqrt(length(x)),col=rust,lty=2)
}
style()
par(mfrow=c(1,2), mar=c(3,3.6,1.4,.5), mgp=c(1.9,.55,0))
corplot(r,title="Training residual ACF",L=36)
corplot(r,TRUE,"Training residual PACF",36)
```

The sample ACF at lags 1–3 is 0.846, 0.653, and 0.509. At lags 12 and 24 it is 0.288 and 0.052. Only the first annual lag exceeds the nominal white-noise guides ($\pm0.146$). The PACF is 0.846 at lag 1 and $-0.220$ at lag 2. At lags 12 and 24 the PACF is $-0.017$ and $-0.069$. Once intervening lags are accounted for, little direct partial correlation remains at either annual lag. The residuals are centered near zero with no strong visible trend or seasonal cycle, so an approximately stationary model is plausible. Some correlation remains at lag 12 (0.288, about twice the $\pm0.146$ guide), so a little seasonality is left over. By lag 24 it is gone. The late-2012 to early-2013 spike and the growing spread, however, could break constant variance. Each plotted ACF pools observations from the entire training period. A single pooled value can hide a correlation that changes between early and late years, so the graph alone cannot establish stationarity.

**What the lags tell us.** A positive lag-1 ACF means that a month above its fitted baseline tends to be followed by another above-baseline month. The lag-2 ACF includes dependence passed through the intervening month. The lag-2 PACF asks what two months ago adds after accounting for last month. The lag-2 PACF can be negative (-0.220) and coexist with a positive lag-2 ACF (0.653). The positive lag-12 ACF warrants checking for annual structure again after fitting the short-lag models.

**Working decision.** We use an undifferenced residual model because deviations repeatedly return toward zero and the ACF declines gradually from its initial peak. Differencing these residuals would change the target to month-to-month changes in those deviations. There is less support for constant variance. The residual standard deviations for the first and last 90 training months are `r fmt(sd(head(r,90)))` and `r fmt(sd(tail(r,90)))` estimated firearms. That comparison is sensitive to the late spikes. We treat stationarity as a working approximation for point forecasts, with greater uncertainty about the size of exceptional errors.

## 6. Three candidate models for the same residual series

```{r candidates, include=FALSE}
orders <- list("AR(2)"=c(2,0,0),"MA(2)"=c(0,0,2),"ARMA(1,1)"=c(1,0,1))
models <- lapply(orders,function(o) arima(r,order=o,method="ML",include.mean=FALSE))
stopifnot(all(vapply(models,function(x) x$code==0, logical(1))))
```

Each candidate is fit to the same 180 residuals. We chose low orders from the Question 5 ACF and PACF (Chapter 3, Lectures 11–14). A pure AR model has a PACF that cuts off and an ACF that tails off. A pure MA model has an ACF that cuts off. A mixed model tails off in both.

*AR(2).* The ACF decays slowly (0.846, 0.653, 0.509). The PACF has two large spikes beyond the $\pm0.146$ bounds, 0.846 at lag 1 and $-0.220$ at lag 2, and then stays within bounds, including at lags 12 ($-0.017$) and 24 ($-0.069$). This points to AR(2). The negative lag-2 value means two months ago has a small negative effect once last month is accounted for.

*MA(2).* An MA(2) needs the ACF to cut off after lag 2, but the lag-3 ACF is still 0.509. A two-term MA also cannot give a lag-1 autocorrelation above about 0.71, and ours is 0.846. We include it as a baseline to test whether two lags of shocks are enough.

*ARMA(1,1).* This is the simplest mixed model. The ACF drops at a steady rate (0.653/0.846 $\approx 0.77$ and 0.509/0.653 $\approx 0.78$), which fits an AR coefficient near 0.77. The MA term gives room to match the high lag-1 value of 0.846.

Let $X_t=\widehat R_t$ in estimated firearms and let $Z_t$ be zero-mean white noise. We fit by Gaussian maximum likelihood with $d=0$ and a fixed zero mean, since the regression already centered the residuals. With R's positive MA sign convention, the fitted equations (coefficients rounded to three decimals) are

$$\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{AR}(2):\quad X_t &= 1.044X_{t-1}-0.230X_{t-2}+Z_t,\\
\mathrm{MA}(2):\quad X_t &= Z_t+1.044Z_{t-1}+0.453Z_{t-2},\\
\mathrm{ARMA}(1,1):\quad X_t &=0.767X_{t-1}+Z_t+0.309Z_{t-1}.
\end{aligned}$$

```{r fitted-table, results='asis'}
tableout(data.frame(Model=names(models),
  'Innovation variance [(firearms/month)^2]'=fmt(sapply(models,function(m) m$sigma2)),
  AIC=fmt(sapply(models,AIC),2), check.names=FALSE))
```

In AR(2), raising last month's deviation by 10,000 while holding the deviation two months ago fixed raises the next prediction by about 10,440. The negative second coefficient adjusts for persistence already present two months earlier. In MA(2), a 10,000 innovation adds about 10,440 one month later and 4,530 two months later, then stops. In ARMA(1,1), it acts through both the last deviation and the last innovation, for an initial response of $(0.767+0.309)10{,}000=10{,}760$. After that, the response shrinks by a factor of 0.767 each month.

Innovation variance is the spread of the one-step forecast errors. The innovation standard deviations are about 78,520 firearms for AR(2), 87,346 for MA(2), and 78,177 for ARMA(1,1). AIC balances fit against the number of estimated parameters. All three models use the same data, mean convention, and parameter count, so their AIC penalties are equal. MA(2)'s AIC is 39.70 above the minimum, and AR(2)'s is 1.55 above ARMA(1,1)'s. Question 7 checks whether the innovations still contain predictable structure.

## 7. Checking the candidate models

The diagnostic series is each model's one-step prediction errors (innovations). A good fit should remove the short-lag dependence seen in Question 5. The panels show the innovation ACFs on a common scale with approximate 95% pointwise white-noise guides.

```{r diagnostic-acfs, fig.height=2}
style()
par(mfrow=c(1,3), mar=c(3,3.3,1.4,.4), mgp=c(1.9,.5,0))
for (name in names(models)) {
  e <- as.numeric(resid(models[[name]]))
  a <- as.numeric(acf(e,lag.max=24,plot=FALSE)$acf)[-1]
  plot(1:24,a,type="h",col=teal,lwd=1.6,xlab="Lag (months)",ylab="ACF (unitless)",
       ylim=c(-.45,.45),main=paste(name, "innovation ACF"),cex.main=.9)
  abline(h=0,col=dark)
  abline(h=c(-1,1)*1.96/sqrt(length(e)),lty=2,col=rust)
}
```

**Ljung–Box test at lag 24.** For each model, $H_0:\rho_1=\cdots=\rho_{24}=0$ for the innovations, and $H_A$ states at least one of these autocorrelations is nonzero. Each candidate estimates two AR/MA coefficients, giving $24-p-q=22$ reference degrees of freedom. For each model test, we compared the observed $Q$ to the upper tail of a $\chi^2_{22}$ distribution. A small p-value indicates more combined autocorrelation than expected under the null. Below is a table of the test statistics, degrees of freedom, p-values, and decisions at the 5% level for our three chosen models.

```{r ljung-box, results='asis'}
lb <- Map(function(model,o) Box.test(resid(model),lag=24,type="Ljung-Box",
                                     fitdf=sum(o[c(1,3)])), models,orders)
pval <- sapply(lb,function(x) x$p.value)
tableout(data.frame(Model=names(models),Q=fmt(sapply(lb,function(x) x$statistic),2),
                    df=sapply(lb,function(x) unname(x$parameter)),
                    'p-value'=formatC(pval,format="g",digits=4),
                    'Decision at 5%'=ifelse(pval<.05,"Reject","Fail to reject"),
                    check.names=FALSE))
eligible <- which(pval >= .05)
winner <- eligible[which.min(sapply(models[eligible],AIC))]
best <- models[[winner]]
```

**AR(2).** With $p=0.391$, the joint test fails to reject the null hypothesis. Lags 12 and 24 cross their pointwise guides, so annual dependence is worth watching even though the joint statistic is unexceptional.

**MA(2).** With $p=3.45\times10^{-10}$, the joint test rejects. Lags 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, and 12 cross the guides. A two-month shock window leaves predictable variation at several lags.

**ARMA(1,1).** With $p=0.403$, the joint test fails to reject. Lags 12 and 24 cross the guides here too. Individual crossings and a non-significant joint test can both happen, because the joint test weighs all 24 lags together against its own reference distribution.

**Model choice.** AR(2) and ARMA(1,1) both pass the joint diagnostic and both use two dependence coefficients. We selected ARMA(1,1) because it has the lower training AIC (4574.25 versus 4575.80) and a slightly smaller innovation standard deviation (78,177 versus 78,520 estimated firearms per month). The AIC difference of 1.55 is a modest preference, so AR(2) remains a credible alternative, and the annual-lag crossings are a limitation of both fits. 

**Spikes remain.** The largest absolute innovation is in December 2012, about `r fmt(max(abs(resid(best)))/sqrt(best$sigma2),1)` innovation standard deviations from zero. Weak autocorrelation can coexist with very large errors, because the test only covers linear dependence. It says nothing about normality, independence, or the cause of the spike. In December 2012, observed sales exceeded the selected model's one-step prediction by about `r fmt(as.numeric(resid(best))[which(train$date==as.Date("2012-12-01"))])` estimated firearms. Even after allowing for December's usual level and recent positive deviations, the surprise is large. This is an in-sample error, since the parameters were estimated from the full training period. Only the 2015 forecasts are scored on data left out of estimation. A short-memory linear ARMA model cannot produce one-off jumps like this, so they remain as outliers. The innovation ACFs also still cross the guides at lags 12 and 24, because the seasonal pattern is not perfectly constant (the December peak grows over time).

## 8. Twelve forecasts from December 2014

```{r forecasting, include=FALSE}
residual.forecast <- as.numeric(predict(best,n.ahead=12)$pred)
forecast <- as.numeric(predict(linear,newdata=test)) + residual.forecast
last.year <- subset(train, year == 2014)
benchmark <- last.year$y[match(test$month.num, last.year$month.num)]
scores <- function(f) {
  error <- test$y-f
  c(MAE=mean(abs(error)), RMSE=sqrt(mean(error^2)))
}
```

Using $T=180$ for December 2014 as the forecast origin, the two forecasting rules over horizons $h=1,\ldots,12$ are$$\widehat Y_{T+h\mid T}=\widehat\beta_0+\widehat\beta_1(T+h)+\widehat\gamma_{m(T+h)}+\widehat X_{T+h\mid T}, \qquad \widehat Y^{\rm benchmark}_{T+h\mid T}=Y_{T+h-12}.$$
The full model combines the projected linear trend and calendar-month effect at $t=180+h$ with the ARMA residual forecast, which shrinks toward zero by a factor of roughly $0.767$ per month after the first step since future innovations are forecast as zero. By contrast, the seasonal naive benchmark simply carries forward the observed sales from the corresponding month of 2014.

```{r forecast-plot, fig.height=2.4}
style()
curves <- cbind(test$y,forecast,benchmark)/1e6
matplot(1:12,curves,type="o",pch=c(16,1,4),lty=c(1,2,3),lwd=1.6,
        col=c(dark,teal,rust),xaxt="n",xlab="Calendar month in 2015",ylab="Sales (million firearms/month)",
     main="2015 U.S. monthly sales: observations and forecasts")
axis(1,1:12,month.abb)
legend("topleft",c("Observed","Linear trend + ARMA","Same month of 2014"),
       col=c(dark,teal,rust),lty=1:3,pch=c(16,1,4),bty="n",cex=.7)
```

For January, the deterministic component is `r fmt(as.numeric(predict(linear,newdata=test))[1])` and the predicted residual is `r fmt(residual.forecast[1])` estimated firearms, which add to `r fmt(forecast[1])`. By December, the residual contribution is only `r fmt(residual.forecast[12])`, so the persistence helps early in the year and then fades. The long-horizon forecast depends almost entirely on the extrapolated baseline and December's usual offset. The seasonal benchmark instead starts from the observed level of each 2014 month. Neither method updates with actual 2015 sales as they arrive.

**Monthly results** 

```{r monthly-forecasts, results='asis'}
half <- function(i) data.frame(Month=month.abb[i],Observed=round(test$y[i]),
                                Model=round(forecast[i]),Benchmark=round(benchmark[i]))
monthly.results <- cbind(half(1:6), half(7:12))
tab <- knitr::kable(monthly.results, format="latex", booktabs=TRUE, row.names=FALSE,
                    linesep="", col.names=rep(c("Month","Observed","Model","Benchmark"),2))
knitr::asis_output(paste0("\\begin{center}\\footnotesize\n", tab, "\n\\end{center}"))
```

**Errors over all 12 months** (estimated firearms per month)

```{r scoring, results='asis'}
score.table <- rbind('Linear trend + ARMA(1,1)'=scores(forecast),
                     'Same month of 2014'=scores(benchmark))
tableout(data.frame(Method=rownames(score.table), MAE=fmt(score.table[,1]),
                    RMSE=fmt(score.table[,2])))
```

For errors $e_h=Y_{180+h}-\widehat Y_{180+h}$, MAE is the average of $|e_h|$ and RMSE is the square root of the average $e_h^2$. The same-month benchmark wins on both measures for 2015. The model overpredicts January through October and underpredicts November and December. Its December miss of about 741,000 estimated firearms is larger than the benchmark's December miss of about 651,000.

Overall, the benchmark reduces MAE by `r fmt(100*(1-score.table[2,1]/score.table[1,1]),1)`% and RMSE by `r fmt(100*(1-score.table[2,2]/score.table[1,2]),1)`%, achieving smaller absolute errors in `r sum(abs(test$y-benchmark)<abs(test$y-forecast))` of the 12 months. While MAE tracks the average error magnitude, RMSE penalizes large misses more heavily by squaring them—making the December 2015 surge (2,350,708 actual) the primary driver of both metrics. The benchmark comes out ahead largely because its biggest misses are less severe, including a roughly 90,000-firearm advantage in December (1,700,097 vs. the model's 1,609,717), though a single holdout year cannot confirm whether this ranking would persist long term.

Furthermore, the model's extrapolated linear trend overshoots early 2015—predicting roughly 1,260,890 in January against an actual of 1,068,401. Because overall sales cooled off following the 2013 surge, anchoring directly to the prior year's 2014 levels aligned much closer with 2015 reality than projecting the multi-year upward trend forward.

## 9. Maryland around the 2013 policy event

Aisch and Keller (2016) identify May 2013 as the month Maryland approved new restrictions. For each Maryland month in 2012–2014, we applied the Question 1 weights to that state’s own checks. For example, September 2013 gives $1.1(38{,}055+9{,}912)+2(17)=52{,}797.7$ estimated firearms. The dotted line marks May approval, and the dashed line marks the October deadline discussed in the article. Plotting both dates lets us see whether the largest change coincided with approval or occurred in the months between.

```{r maryland, fig.height=2.4}
md <- subset(raw,state=="Maryland" & year>=2012 & year<=2014)
md <- md[order(md$date),]
style()
plot(md$date,md$y/1000,type="o",pch=16,cex=.5,col=teal,
     main="Maryland estimated monthly firearm sales, 2012-2014",
     ylab="Sales (thousand firearms/month)",xlab="Calendar month",xaxt="n")
ticks <- seq(as.Date("2012-01-01"),as.Date("2014-07-01"),by="6 months")
axis.Date(1,at=ticks,format="%b %Y")
abline(v=as.Date("2013-05-01"),lty=3)
abline(v=as.Date("2013-10-01"),lty=2,col=rust)
legend("topleft", c("May approval","October deadline"),
       lty=c(3,2), col=c("black",rust), bty="n", cex=.7)
```

Estimated sales fell from 15,433 in May to 13,113 in July, then reached 52,798 in September before dropping to 21,381 in October. September was the last full month before the October deadline. The 2013 series stays at around 13,000 to 20,000 until the sharp jump in September 2013. August 2013 was 15,975, and after, the October sales drift back to normal. The timing is consistent with buyers moving purchases forward, but these monthly counts contain no information about individual buyers’ motives. Maryland alone supplies no estimate of what September sales would have been without the policy. Nationwide demand, seasonal buying, or shifts in the timing of purchases could also affect the series. We chose Maryland because the monthly approval date permits a before-and-after comparison within the event year, and the surrounding years also let us compare September with the same calendar month. Maryland's September estimates were 10,220 in 2012, 52,798 in 2013, and 7,813 in 2014. The 2013 peak was more than five times the previous September's level. That comparison helps distinguish an exceptional September from an ordinary recurring fall peak. However, this change cannot be automatically by interpreted as causal. The article says buyers rushed to beat the October deadline after the law passed. This is one plausible explanation for the jump, but the data alone cannot separate it from other causes. Other national factors, such as the surge after Sandy Hook in December 2012 and January 2013, also affect the 2013 series. There is no comparison group, and Maryland alone gives no estimate of September sales without the policy. Background checks are not completed sales, and national demand, seasonal buying, or shifts in purchase timing could also move the series.

## 10. Conclusions

Estimated U.S. firearm sales combined a rising long-run level with a recurring calendar pattern. In the training years, December averaged about 1.25 million firearms per month, more than twice the June average. December 2012 stood out even among Decembers. The fitted linear trend rose by about 44,018 firearms per month each year, but multi-year runs of negative residuals show the limits of a constant slope. The month indicators removed the average calendar pattern, yet residuals one year apart still had a correlation of 0.288.

Departures from the baseline carried over between adjacent months. AR(2) and ARMA(1,1) both passed the joint innovation check, though correlations at the annual lags stayed visible. ARMA(1,1) had the lowest training AIC. December 2012 still produced an error about seven innovation standard deviations above zero. In 2015, the selected model overpredicted January through October and missed the December surge by about 741,000 firearms. Repeating each corresponding 2014 observation cut the mean absolute error from about 132,368 to 108,228 firearms per month. Each method was closer in six months, so this only ranks the two for one forecast year.

Two limitations affect interpretation. First, background checks measure transactions imperfectly. Some private sales are absent, and fixed conversion factors cannot recover how many firearms changed hands in each transaction (Aisch and Keller, 2016). Forecast errors therefore describe errors in the estimated series. Second, the Maryland comparison has no untreated comparison group. A spike after policy approval gives its timing, but concurrent national changes or buyers shifting purchases between months could produce a similar pattern.

  print(which(abs(a) > 1.96/sqrt(length(resid(m)))))
}

                 standardized=e[peak]/sqrt(best$sigma2)))
